questions.stem:
The clocks at the tram depot used to be checked against one another once a month. That was adequate when tickets showed only the date, but a passenger now has precisely 45 minutes to change trams on one fare. Two clocks can agree with one another and still both be wrong. Adding another clock at the busiest platform would make it easier to see the time, but would not settle disputes about it. The depot should set all its clocks to a single external time signal before services begin each day.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: The depot should synchronise its clocks to one outside signal each day.
options.B: The depot's clocks can agree and still show the wrong time.
options.C: The busiest platform should have an extra clock.
options.D: Passengers should be given longer to change trams.
options.E: Checking the clocks once a month was adequate for the old tickets.

questions.explanation: The other claims explain why mutual agreement and visibility are not enough. The specific measure they support is daily synchronisation to an external signal.

questions.stem:
The park's ornamental pond should not be cleared of fallen branches this winter. Branches above the water allow birds to perch away from the busy footpath. Under the surface, their forks trap dead leaves in places where small animals can feed. It is true that a pond almost completely covered in branches would be less attractive to visitors. This one, however, has enough open water to reflect the surrounding trees, and staff can remove an individual branch if it presents a hazard. A general clearance would sacrifice the benefits without solving a current problem.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: Submerged branches collect leaves that some animals can feed on.
options.B: Staff ought never to remove any branch.
options.C: There is still open water in the pond.
options.D: The park should leave most fallen branches in the pond this winter.
options.E: The pond should be judged on its wildlife rather than its appearance alone.

questions.explanation: The reasons and the safety qualification support leaving the branches generally in place, not banning removal of individual hazards.

questions.stem:
A dictionary team needs to decide what to do with interviews recorded for a regional pronunciation project. A written transcript is useful for finding a word, but it rarely records the exact sound, and the sounds were the reason for interviewing people in the first place. Not every recording is clear enough to be worth keeping. Nonetheless, a future researcher cannot use better listening equipment on a recording that no longer exists. The team should therefore keep usable recordings as well as the transcripts, even if the written material is what most visitors consult.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: The team should replace transcripts with recordings.
options.B: The project should retain its usable recordings alongside the written transcripts.
options.C: Some recordings are too unclear to retain.
options.D: Written transcripts make searching for a word easier.
options.E: Future researchers are likely to have better equipment.

questions.explanation: The passage weighs searchable transcripts against the evidence only audio preserves. Neither is proposed as a replacement for the other.

questions.stem:
One objection to moving the amateur football final back by two hours is that the later kick-off would make it harder for children to attend. That is a good reason not to move the match permanently. This Saturday, however, the athletics club will be dismantling equipment at the only other ground with floodlights. The referee has ruled the original pitch unsafe until a strip of damaged turf is repaired, and the repair cannot finish before the old kick-off. A later start this Saturday is preferable to calling off the final altogether.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: Children's attendance would suffer if the kick-off were permanently later.
options.B: The athletics club should use a different venue.
options.C: A fixture depends on the referee finding the pitch safe.
options.D: The damaged strip should be repaired before the old kick-off.
options.E: For this Saturday only, the final should start later rather than be cancelled.

questions.explanation: The concern about children limits the recommendation to this Saturday. The other constraints explain why delaying is better than cancelling.

questions.stem:
An exhibition of woven work currently gives every object a single year, even where the maker is known to have worked on it over several winters. The simplicity makes the labels easy to scan, but it can lead visitors to infer that a new design appeared only after another displayed beside it. In several cases the evidence shows that work on the two designs overlapped. The labels should give a range of years wherever the evidence indicates extended production. This is no objection to using a single date when there is good evidence for one.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: The exhibition should list objects in order of completion.
options.B: Visitors sometimes mistake a date on a label for the start of production.
options.C: The labels should use date ranges for objects known to have been made over several years.
options.D: Several of the exhibited designs were produced at overlapping times.
options.E: Every object label should give a range, even if the exact year is known.

questions.explanation: The possible misreading of a single year supports using a range when production extended across years. The closing qualification rules out a blanket change.

questions.stem:
A proposal to cut the price of water for every factory in the district has been defended on the ground that it would help struggling employers. Certainly the smallest employers would welcome lower bills, but the factories using the most water would receive the largest reductions, including some that are making record profits. Nor is water use a reliable indication of how many jobs are at risk. If support is justified, the district should decide who receives it using evidence about financial need rather than giving every factory cheaper water.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: The smallest employers are likely to welcome lower bills.
options.B: Any justified support should be targeted by financial need rather than provided through a universal water discount.
options.C: Factories using the most water should be denied any assistance.
options.D: Water consumption is not a dependable measure of jobs at risk.
options.E: No employer should receive public support at present.

questions.explanation: The argument challenges the allocation of a proposed subsidy, not the legitimacy of all subsidies. Need is offered as the better criterion.

questions.stem:
When a radio station broadcasts a pre-recorded interview, it may remove pauses to make the programme fit its slot. But a long pause before an answer can show that the question was unexpected, whereas a brief hesitation in the middle of a sentence can simply be a search for a word. Listeners cannot recover a pause they never hear. Editors should distinguish between pauses that help convey how an exchange took place and those that do not, rather than trimming every silence to the same duration.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: Pre-recorded interviews sometimes need editing to fit a broadcast slot.
options.B: Every long pause is evidence that a question took the speaker by surprise.
options.C: Silence can tell the listener something about an exchange.
options.D: Editors should preserve pauses that matter to the meaning of an interview rather than shorten all pauses alike.
options.E: Interviews should always be broadcast live.

questions.explanation: The contrasting examples establish why a uniform trimming rule is unsuitable. They support selective editing, not a ban on editing.

questions.stem:
A travelling display can sometimes borrow a valuable original for little more than the cost of transporting a replica. The organiser should still prefer the replica if visitors chiefly need to see how the object works. With the original, wardens would have to prevent handling, which would leave the most instructive feature hidden behind glass. It is true that some visitors value encountering a piece of the past, and an original can justify extra precautions when that encounter is the point of the display. That is not the purpose of this display.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: For this display, the organiser should choose the replica even if borrowing the original is almost as cheap.
options.B: Wardens ought to let visitors handle valuable originals when that is educational.
options.C: The educational value of this object lies largely in demonstrating its operation.
options.D: Some visitors value seeing a historical original.
options.E: Replicas should be preferred at every travelling exhibition.

questions.explanation: The recommendation appears near the start; the handling constraint and the final qualification support it specifically for this display.

questions.stem:
The council is considering making every street nameplate the same height. A uniform height makes inspection easier, and normally the easier a sign is to find, the more useful it is. At several junctions, however, an old wall hides a street nameplate from approaching pedestrians at the proposed height. Moving it a little higher makes it visible from both footpaths. Consistency might remain a sensible starting point, but it should not prevent borough engineers from choosing a different height where the standard would make a sign harder to see.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: Engineers should be able to depart from the standard height when it would impair a sign's visibility.
options.B: Nameplates should have no standard height anywhere.
options.C: Making signs easy to find increases their usefulness.
options.D: Uniform height makes inspection easier.
options.E: The walls that hide nameplates should be removed.

questions.explanation: The argument accepts a default height but says the purpose of the signs justifies exceptions. The examples support that qualified policy.

questions.stem:
A literary journal lets its reviewers remain anonymous to prevent writers retaliating over unfavourable reviews. The policy addresses a real concern. But a review that names a writer's supposed employer or alleges a conflict of interest makes claims that could damage that writer independently of the judgement on the book. Such claims do not become suitable just because the rest of the review is well argued. The journal should check the factual claims in anonymous reviews before publication, instead of treating anonymity and the quality of the literary argument as sufficient safeguards.

Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.A: Anonymity can protect a reviewer from retaliation.
options.B: All anonymous reviews should be prohibited.
options.C: A book review may cause harm unrelated to the judgement of the book.
options.D: A well-argued review is more useful to readers than a personal attack.
options.E: The journal should verify factual claims in anonymous reviews before publishing them.

questions.explanation: The potential harm is a reason to verify factual claims, not to identify the reviewers or to stop publishing their opinions.

questions.stem:
For a survey of a coastal dune, volunteers marked flowering plants in two equal plots. The registrar instructed them to mark every dune daisy they saw, including plants outside the tracks, but not to mark plants they could not identify. In the eastern plot they recorded twelve confirmed daisies and in the western plot they recorded none. Some flowering plants in the west were too far from the track to identify confidently. The volunteers were trained to tell daisies from other plants before the survey.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: No dune daisies were present in the western plot.
options.B: There were exactly twelve daisies on the whole dune.
options.C: The eastern plot had more daisies than the western plot.
options.D: Every unidentified plant in the west was a dune daisy.
options.E: At least twelve dune daisies were present in the eastern plot.

questions.explanation: The twelve confirmed records establish a minimum in the east. Unidentified plants prevent a conclusion about the true number in the west or the overall total.

questions.stem:
A station loans umbrellas to passengers. Every umbrella currently on loan has its station number written on the inside of the handle, including those borrowed before the present management arrived. The same station numbers also appear on a batch of umbrellas which the station sold off last year; the station did not remove the numbers before selling them. An attendant finds an umbrella with the station number at the back of a taxi. There is no further record on the umbrella showing why it left.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: The number alone cannot establish whether this umbrella is currently on loan.
options.B: The umbrella must have been borrowed from the station.
options.C: The umbrella must have been sold off last year.
options.D: Only umbrellas borrowed under the present management carry numbers.
options.E: A missing umbrella can always be traced to its borrower using the number.

questions.explanation: Both borrowed and sold umbrellas may bear the number. Neither status follows solely from seeing it.

questions.stem:
For a study of an office atrium, an engineer placed one thermometer over the entrance and one below the glass roof. Both proved accurate when tested after the experiment. At midday the lower thermometer registered 19 degrees and the upper registered 25 degrees. The engineer also noted that both temperatures had been lower shortly after sunrise. Nobody measured the air midway between the thermometers. On the day in question the atrium was used by staff as usual, including for a meeting that began at noon.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: At midday the whole upper half of the atrium was warmer than the whole lower half.
options.B: At midday the air at the upper measurement point was warmer than at the lower point.
options.C: The meeting caused the temperature difference.
options.D: A thermometer halfway up would have shown 22 degrees.
options.E: The difference between the two readings was greatest at midday.

questions.explanation: The reported readings compare two points at midday. They do not establish the profile between them, the cause, or when the difference peaked.

questions.stem:
A town charges businesses for permits to put seats on the pavement. Any permit granted after April requires a clear route to the kerb. A permit granted before May continues until its expiry even if there is no such route, unless it is revoked for another reason. One restaurant is putting out seats with a permit that the licensing officer confirms is current and not revoked. There is no clear route to the kerb beside the restaurant, and the officer confirms that it has complied with all conditions of its permit.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: The restaurant was not allowed to put seats out before May.
options.B: The permit was granted in April.
options.C: All restaurants with permits lack clear routes to the kerb.
options.D: The restaurant will never need to provide a clear route.
options.E: The permit was not granted after April.

questions.explanation: A later permit would require the route that is absent. Nothing identifies a particular earlier month or guarantees the restaurant's future position.

questions.stem:
A bowls club compared the membership lists from before and after its pavilion repairs. Everyone on the old list renewed except six people who had moved away. The new list is longer than the old one. The two lists use the same definition of membership and list each person only once. The club had not kept a separate record of why new members joined, and it had advertised in local shops as well as reopening the pavilion. Its treasurer wants to know what the lists alone show.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: The pavilion repairs increased membership.
options.B: Exactly six people joined the club after the repairs.
options.C: More people saw the shop adverts than used the pavilion.
options.D: More than six people on the new list were not on the old one.
options.E: Six is the total number of people who have ever left the club.

questions.explanation: Six names were lost, so more than six must have been added for the list to grow. The lists cannot tell us why people joined.

questions.stem:
A harbour improvement fund accepts pledges in two forms. A conditional pledge counts towards the published target only after the stated condition is met. An unconditional pledge counts immediately, even though it may not be paid until work begins. On Monday the harbour authority added a particular pledge to the published target total. That donor had not paid any of it by Tuesday. The authority says the addition on Monday followed its ordinary rules, and no money from that donor was counted twice.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: The donor must have made an unconditional pledge.
options.B: The pledge either had no condition or had already met its condition by Monday.
options.C: The harbour should treat every conditional pledge as unpaid.
options.D: The condition must have been met on Monday itself.
options.E: The Monday total measures money already in the fund's bank account.

questions.explanation: Both kinds of pledge can count before payment. A conditional one could count only if its condition was satisfied by the time it was added.

questions.stem:
A conservator working on an old town hall found stamped tiles marked with different workshops' names. The workshop that used the stamp H operated only after the fire of 1864. Two H tiles are embedded in a roof section, and records show the tiles were in that section when it was erected, not inserted by later repairers. Other tiles in the section have no visible stamp, and old tiles from another building were sometimes reused by roofers. No account has been found giving the date of the construction work.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: All of its tiles were produced by workshop H.
options.B: The fire destroyed every section of the original roof.
options.C: The roof section was erected after the fire of 1864.
options.D: The hall itself was first built after 1864.
options.E: The older tiles in the section were necessarily reused from another building.

questions.explanation: The H tiles could not have existed before the fire and were already present when the section was built. This dates the section, not the whole hall.

questions.stem:
A cycle storage scheme records every alarm from its motion sensors, including accidental activations. An alarm is listed as verified only when someone checks the rack and confirms that a bicycle has been moved without permission. It is then listed as resolved only when the missing bicycle is located. The report for June lists twenty alarms, of which eight were verified and five resolved. Each alarm appears once in the twenty, and no alarm was later moved to a different month for reporting purposes.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: Exactly twelve of the alarms were caused by accidental activations.
options.B: Three of the alarms were verified but not listed as resolved.
options.C: Fifteen bicycles were stolen and never located.
options.D: Five June alarms were resolved without anyone checking the rack.
options.E: Every unverified alarm was later resolved.

questions.explanation: Resolution is a further classification for a verified alarm. Subtract the five resolved alarms from the eight verified alarms.

questions.stem:
A wildlife trust estimates the number of nests in a marsh using aerial images. Every nest it counts has to be visible in both sets of images, one taken at dawn and one at dusk. This rule prevents some mistakes but can miss nests concealed at either time. After a storm, the trust counted fewer nests than in its previous survey. Looking at the images, it found that the number visible at dawn had actually increased. It did not separately report how many were visible at dusk.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: The storm destroyed some nests.
options.B: Fewer nests were visible at dusk after the storm.
options.C: Fewer nests satisfied the trust's two-image rule after the storm.
options.D: More nests existed in the marsh after the storm.
options.E: The new dawn images were more accurate than the previous ones.

questions.explanation: The published count is the intersection of nests visible at the two times. A smaller intersection does not establish how the dusk total or the actual population changed.

questions.stem:
An archive exhibits a letter only if the author signed it or the archive can attribute it through other records. If the author is alive, the archive must also obtain permission. It labels every exhibit with the author's name unless the author requested anonymity or the exhibit forms part of an exchange with another archive, in which case the lender's label is retained. Requesting anonymity does not count as giving permission to exhibit. One unsigned letter has been exhibited without its author's name. The archivist confirms that it was not acquired through an exchange and that the archive followed all these rules. Nothing has been published about whether the author is still alive.

Which of the following conclusions can reliably be drawn from the above argument?

options.A: The author gave permission to exhibit, but the archive has no evidence attributing the letter through other records.
options.B: The archive could have withheld a name simply because it had not established an attribution.
options.C: The author's request to remain anonymous made separate permission unnecessary if the author was alive.
options.D: The archive has attributed the letter through other records, and the author requested anonymity.
options.E: The archive must know the author's name and must have obtained permission to exhibit.

questions.explanation: The lack of a signature requires independent attribution; the lack of a name, with no exchange, requires a request for anonymity. Permission is required only for a living author.

questions.stem:
At present a teacher sends pupils a new spelling list each Friday. Several pupils lose the loose sheet, and when the teacher quizzes them the following week they say they could not remember which words to practise. The teacher plans to let each pupil copy the list into a small notebook that stays in their school bag. The notebook will not change the words tested or the format of the quiz. Yet by making the list reliably available, the change should result in more pupils practising before the quiz.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: Every pupil who does not practise has lost the loose sheet.
options.B: Some pupils who would lose the loose sheet will practise when they can consult the notebook.
options.C: The quizzes test only words pupils have taken down correctly.
options.D: Notebooks cost less than printing weekly lists.
options.E: The pupils who already practise will practise for longer.

questions.explanation: Reliable access will change practice only if at least some pupils use lists they would otherwise have lost.

questions.stem:
The community clinic offers advice by telephone on weekday mornings. Some callers who speak little English give up before they can explain why they are ringing. The reception team could add an option that lets callers reach an interpreter before they speak to a clinician. The clinic does not propose to extend its morning hours, and it will keep the ordinary menu for callers who do not need interpretation. By making the new option available, the clinic can help at least some of those callers obtain advice that they currently miss.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: No caller who speaks little English currently receives useful advice.
options.B: Every interpreter must have previous clinical experience.
options.C: English speakers will be connected faster under the new menu.
options.D: Callers generally prefer speaking to a clinician in the morning.
options.E: At least some callers who would otherwise give up will be able to use the interpretation option.

questions.explanation: An option that the intended callers cannot use cannot help them reach a clinician. The argument requires some benefit, not that it reaches every caller.

questions.stem:
Residents requesting an allotment usually take the first site offered because turning it down means returning to the end of the waiting list. Several gardeners consequently travel across town to plots near other gardeners' homes. Giving up a plot and reapplying would risk a long wait, so the distances persist. The association is considering a service that lets two tenants exchange plots directly if both agree. By matching tenants through that service, it could reduce some journeys without creating any new plots or changing the waiting list for applicants.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: All tenants would prefer the closest plot to the one they have now.
options.B: The waiting list is longer near the centre of town.
options.C: There are at least two tenants for whom a mutually acceptable exchange would shorten their journeys overall.
options.D: Plots at different sites command identical annual rents.
options.E: New applicants value short journeys more than established gardeners do.

questions.explanation: The service can shorten total travel only if there is a mutually acceptable match that does so. The reported cross-town journeys don't establish that on their own.

questions.stem:
At a two-day festival, stewards currently stamp hands on Saturday so visitors can return on Sunday. The ink wears off when some people wash their hands, and the checks then hold up the entrance. The festival manager proposes paper wristbands worn continuously over both days. She expects fewer visitors to have to explain their missing stamp, so fewer legitimate visitors will be stopped for extra checks. The number of entrances, the staffing levels and the way Sunday-only tickets are sold would all stay as they are.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: A wristband will be cheaper than ink for every visitor.
options.B: Nobody will ever be able to transfer a wristband to another person.
options.C: Enough legitimate visitors will still have legible wristbands on Sunday to reduce the number needing extra checks.
options.D: Stewards always check the hands of Sunday-only visitors too.
options.E: The Sunday entrance queue will be shorter than the Saturday queue.

questions.explanation: The prediction depends on the replacement credential surviving better in practice, not on wristbands preventing all misuse.

questions.stem:
A metalworking firm finds that its trainees rarely learn how to diagnose faults: their usual job is to carry out repairs after an experienced worker has investigated. The firm proposes assigning each trainee one quiet shift a month to shadow the worker who first examines a fault. The worker would keep responsibility for the decision, so the planned change would not affect who signs off expensive work. Management expects trainees to diagnose future faults more successfully after watching the investigations than they do after simply carrying out the repairs.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: Trainees can learn something about diagnosing faults from observing the investigations they will attend.
options.B: Experienced workers always identify the fault correctly on their first attempt.
options.C: Faults on quiet shifts are more costly than those on busy shifts.
options.D: Trainees cannot learn anything useful from repairing faults already diagnosed.
options.E: A trainee will qualify sooner if allowed to sign off expensive work.

questions.explanation: The recommendation assumes observation can teach at least some useful diagnostic skills. Otherwise the change does not address the stated problem.

questions.stem:
An engineer has proposed fitting washable screens to the ventilation openings of a school gym. Tests on a spare opening showed that the screens caught most of the test pollen and restricted airflow only slightly when new. The gym currently closes for some lessons when airborne pollen levels inside become too high. The manager wants to fit the screens and clean them every Friday, arguing that this will keep the gym usable more often without breaching the minimum fresh-air requirement, including on the days just before the weekly clean.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: The screens will catch every kind of airborne particle equally well.
options.B: By the end of a weekly cleaning cycle the screens will still allow enough fresh air into the gym.
options.C: The gym would stay open regardless of airflow if the pollen level fell.
options.D: Friday is currently the least popular day for gym lessons.
options.E: The screens are the least expensive way to reduce indoor pollen.

questions.explanation: The fresh-air claim is about the whole week, but the airflow test used only a fresh screen. The proposal requires sufficient airflow even before cleaning.

questions.stem:
A village uses the fee from its pedestrian bridge to pay for repainting. In recent years the fee has covered the work, but it is unpopular with residents who cross twice a day. An adviser proposes waiving the fee for residents while raising it for visitors. She estimates that with last year's visitor numbers the new visitor fee alone would have met the repainting bill. On that basis she argues that the change can cover the next repainting entirely from bridge fees, without restoring the charge for residents.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: No visitor will decide against crossing because of the higher fee.
options.B: Enough paying visitors will still cross at the new fee to meet the next repainting bill.
options.C: Residents cross the bridge more often than visitors do.
options.D: The next repainting will cost exactly the same as the last.
options.E: The adviser could have estimated last year's numbers from ticket stubs.

questions.explanation: A higher price applied to old visitor numbers does not establish future revenue. Enough paying visitors are required, even if some stop crossing.

questions.stem:
A college plans to replace handwritten signatures on course certificates with an online verification number. Checking the number on the college's website will confirm that the certificate appears in its record. Employers have complained that unfamiliar signatures are hard to authenticate, so the college argues that the new method will make it easier to tell that a certificate actually belongs to the applicant who presents it. The check will be available to any employer free of charge, and the search screen will not display marks or disciplinary records.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: Employers can tell whether a certificate is genuine just by looking at its number.
options.B: Handwritten signatures have never helped an employer detect a forgery.
options.C: Employers need applicants' marks in order to verify their certificates.
options.D: The college will stop printing the names of course tutors on certificates.
options.E: The verification check gives employers enough information to link the recorded certificate to the particular applicant.

questions.explanation: Verifying that a certificate exists is not equivalent to identifying its owner. Some usable link between the record and the applicant is assumed.

questions.stem:
Neighbours disputing the maintenance of a shared wall can currently ask the council to arrange mediation only after both have agreed in writing. A councillor proposes allowing either neighbour to request an appointment; the other person would remain free to refuse to attend. The council has enough appointments to do this without delays. The councillor argues that the change will settle some disputes that are unresolved under the current system, even though no new power to compel cooperation would be granted to the council or to the person requesting mediation.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: Making attendance compulsory would settle every dispute.
options.B: Most neighbours who use mediation disagree about shared walls.
options.C: The new system will reduce the total number of applications for mediation.
options.D: Some disputes stalled at the consent stage could be settled if an appointment could be offered before the second neighbour formally agreed.
options.E: The people who refused to sign would all attend if given an appointment.

questions.explanation: Removing the initial agreement requirement helps only if it changes the course of at least some disputes; attendance and successful mediation still have to be possible.

questions.stem:
A regional health authority is considering adding a mobile dialysis unit to its existing service. An adviser compared home addresses with the proposed stops and found that every patient currently travelling over an hour lives nearer to a stop than to the hospital. She recommends the unit as a way of cutting the total time that this group spends travelling to treatment. Patients would be free to keep their hospital appointments rather than switch. The proposed stops have not yet been given opening times, but the frequency and duration of each patient's treatment would not change. The adviser has used distance alone to estimate which journeys would be quicker.

Which of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.A: No patient using a proposed stop will have to change buses on the way there.
options.B: Every patient currently travelling over an hour will find the nearest stop quicker to reach.
options.C: Most patients who currently travel less than an hour will keep their hospital appointments.
options.D: The mobile unit would be able to treat every patient in the group if they all chose to switch.
options.E: At least some patients in the group could and would switch to stops that take less time to reach than the hospital.

questions.explanation: Geographical proximity need not translate into a quicker journey or usable appointment. With no reduction in the number of treatments, cutting this group's travel time requires some patients actually to switch to quicker journeys.

questions.stem:
A horticulture tutor wants to improve the success of a difficult seed in the college greenhouse. Even when the soil stays moist, many of the seeds show no sign of absorbing water. Their outer coats are unusually hard. The tutor suspects that opening a tiny gap in the outer coat before sowing would help the seeds take up water and germinate. She is not proposing to change the compost or turn up the heat, because other seeds in the same greenhouse germinate without those measures.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: The hard seed coat can survive transport in a dry box.
options.B: Some seeds with soft coats need warmer compost.
options.C: The college owns equipment for checking greenhouse temperatures.
options.D: Most seeds are sown outdoors instead of in greenhouses.
options.E: In a test using the same soil and temperature, seeds with a tiny cut in the coat germinated more often than uncut seeds from the same batch.

questions.explanation: A controlled comparison directly supports the proposed benefit of opening the coat.

questions.stem:
A club organises evening rides along a canal. Several riders report having difficulty seeing the path immediately after meeting another bicycle whose lamp points straight ahead. There is no street lighting along much of the route. The club proposes asking its riders to point their lamps slightly downwards. It argues that this will make encounters safer, provided riders can still see far enough to stop before obstacles. The request would apply to all club rides on the canal, not to rides on bright city streets.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: The club spends less on lamps than on helmets.
options.B: On the same dark path, downward-angled lamps reduced glare for oncoming riders while still lighting the full stopping distance.
options.C: Most riders own more than one bicycle light.
options.D: Riders who use urban cycle lanes report few problems with glare.
options.E: Downward-angled lamps use a little more power on some settings.

questions.explanation: The finding supports both parts of the proposal: reduced glare and enough forward visibility to stop.

questions.stem:
At present, people waiting to speak at a small claims hearing sit near the courtroom door. On busy days it opens repeatedly and they have trouble hearing when their case is called. A court officer suggests placing a display in the waiting area showing which case is about to start. She thinks this will reduce interruptions to hearings from staff searching for people who have missed the oral announcement. The court would still announce cases aloud and would use reference numbers instead of litigants' names on the display.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: Most oral announcements currently give the names of both parties.
options.B: Nearby courts use public screens to display general directions.
options.C: Courtroom doors are expensive to replace.
options.D: Reference numbers are normally assigned weeks before the hearing.
options.E: Nearly all the people previously missed in this way were in the waiting area and could see the proposed display location.

questions.explanation: A display can help only if the people missing the announcements are in a position to see it. This finding connects the remedy to the missed calls.

questions.stem:
A valley's flood warning system sounds the same siren from every village tower. Residents closer to the river are often the first to hear it, but they cannot tell whether the threat is local or farther down the valley. A volunteer group suggests recording spoken messages for the existing loudspeakers to name the stretches at risk. The group predicts fewer unnecessary journeys to emergency shelters, without making residents less likely to leave when their own village is threatened. It proposes keeping the current siren before each message.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: Several village towers can be seen from the riverside.
options.B: In a rehearsal using the existing equipment, residents reliably distinguished warnings for their own village from warnings for others.
options.C: Many residents have never used an emergency shelter.
options.D: A recorded message takes longer to play than a siren alone.
options.E: The loudspeakers have worked for more than ten years.

questions.explanation: The rehearsal tests whether the added message makes the location clear, which is the link between the change and the proposed benefit.

questions.stem:
Staff at a pharmacy have noticed that some customers buy two different cold remedies without realising both contain the same painkiller. The legal ingredient lists are clear when read carefully, but customers often compare the brand names and the symptoms listed on the front of the packs instead. The pharmacy wants to add a shelf label beside every product containing that painkiller, using the same prominent symbol. It claims that this will prevent some purchases of overlapping remedies, even though it cannot control which products customers use at home.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: When the symbol's meaning was displayed beside trial packs, shoppers preparing to buy two remedies more often recognised that both contained the same painkiller.
options.B: Different brands sometimes use similar colours on their packs.
options.C: Many medicines are sold in supermarkets as well as pharmacies.
options.D: Not every consumer follows instructions after buying cold remedies.
options.E: Some customers find written dosage instructions easier to understand than diagrams.

questions.explanation: The trial shows the proposed cue helps at the point of comparison. That is more directly relevant to purchases than general facts about packaging or use.

questions.stem:
The public library plans to offer a one-week amnesty on overdue charges. Its director says the point is not to collect more fines after the amnesty ends, but to recover books needed by other borrowers. At present, some people with long-overdue books avoid the desk because they expect a bill they cannot afford. During the amnesty they could hand the books in without paying. The director argues that the short-term cost in waived charges is worth paying for the extra books returned to use.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: A similar library's trial recovered many overdue books from borrowers who said a charge had kept them from returning them.
options.B: A new book costs more to catalogue than a returned one.
options.C: Some borrowers have never paid a charge at either library.
options.D: The library raises much less from charges than from public funding.
options.E: Other libraries usually send overdue reminders by email.

questions.explanation: Comparable evidence links the waiver to the precise obstacle identified and records the desired outcome rather than just changes in revenue.

questions.stem:
A small theatre wants to take its productions to villages without a hall equipped for drama. It can buy a portable stage that packs into its existing van. The stage is smaller than the theatre's usual one, so some scenery would have to be redesigned. The producer argues that this cost is worthwhile because the portable stage would make performances possible in venues that the company has declined solely for lack of a usable stage. Performances in the theatre's home town would continue as before.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: The company rarely fills every seat at its home theatre.
options.B: Professional actors often rehearse on a smaller area than they perform on.
options.C: The current van has room for some costumes as well as the stage.
options.D: Audits of recently rejected venues found that most have adequate space, access and facilities for exactly this portable stage.
options.E: The village performances could use the company's ordinary publicity artwork.

questions.explanation: The audits test whether the proposed equipment would actually make the rejected venues usable. That is the benefit offered to justify the redesign.

questions.stem:
A regional concert promoter is considering replacing disposable drink cups with reusable ones. The new cups need to be washed after each show and carried between venues. The promoter says that if most are returned, making fewer replacement cups should more than offset the climate impact of washing and transport. The tickets could include a refund at the exit for every cup handed back. The promoter's environmental case concerns greenhouse gas emissions over several seasons, rather than the appearance of the grounds on the morning after a show.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: A trial with that refund recovered enough cups that measured washing, transport and replacement emissions were lower than under the disposable system.
options.B: Cleanup crews prefer picking up intact cups to picking up shards of plastic.
options.C: Concertgoers can tell which cups belong to the promoter by their colour.
options.D: Some venues currently buy their disposable cups in bulk.
options.E: The cups can be stored outdoors if they are packed in sealed boxes.

questions.explanation: The trial addresses both whether the refund yields enough returns and whether those returns produce the claimed net emissions saving.

questions.stem:
A city museum presently offers audio descriptions through handsets given out at the entrance. The exhibit team wants to add a short spoken overview that tells listeners which features of the room to notice before they reach individual objects. It predicts that people using audio descriptions will then be better able to choose an order in which to explore, rather than following the printed sequence by default. The overview will be optional, and none of the existing descriptions will be removed or shortened as a result.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: Visitors who seldom use the handsets are more familiar with the printed sequence.
options.B: The museum plans to change the wall colour in the room.
options.C: In matched trials, listeners offered an overview chose routes consistent with their own stated interests more often than those given descriptions alone.
options.D: Some visitors take longer to read about an object than to hear about it.
options.E: The optional overview would take under two minutes to play.

questions.explanation: Choosing routes that reflect individual interests directly supports the claim that the overview helps listeners plan their exploration.

questions.stem:
A rail operator proposes replacing calendar-based inspections of some carriage doors with a schedule triggered by the number of openings. Doors in service on suburban lines open far more often in a week than those on long-distance services. The operator says its new schedule would find worn moving parts sooner without increasing the total number of inspections, which would instead be redistributed between the two kinds of service. Electrical checks that are already conducted separately would continue on their existing schedule, regardless of how often each door is opened.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.A: On long-distance journeys the operator sometimes carries fewer passengers than on suburban ones.
options.B: Electrical faults can occur in doors that have rarely opened.
options.C: The operator owns enough spare doors to replace several at once.
options.D: Calendar inspections were introduced when all routes used the same rolling stock.
options.E: Service records show that moving-part wear closely tracks the number of openings and that many calendar inspections take place well before wear appears.

questions.explanation: The records support using openings to predict wear and suggest existing inspection effort can be shifted from low-use doors.

questions.stem:
Conservators at a museum noticed that a set of paper prints curled on the days when more visitors entered the room. A curator suggests that the visitors' breath raised the humidity sufficiently to distort the paper. On that basis she recommends reducing the number of visitors admitted at a time, rather than changing how the prints are mounted. The prints were examined in their existing mounts throughout the period, and the usual opening hours and arrangements for cleaning the room remained unchanged during those weeks.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: Some of the prints are larger than others.
options.B: Admission to the room is included in the ordinary museum ticket.
options.C: On busy days staff spend more time answering visitors' questions.
options.D: Independent readings showed that the air around the prints was no more humid on crowded days than on quiet ones.
options.E: Paper can sometimes be damaged by very high humidity.

questions.explanation: If crowding did not raise the humidity at the prints, the proposed explanation—and hence the case for limiting access—is substantially weakened.

questions.stem:
A machine shop offers cash overtime payments to workers who take an extra Saturday shift. A manager proposes offering a voucher of the same face value for a local supermarket instead. She argues that most workers already buy groceries and can therefore use the vouchers just as easily as cash. She expects the same number of people to volunteer on Saturdays, although the payment method would change for every shift. The proposal would not affect the ordinary wages workers receive for their regular hours from Monday to Friday.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: The supermarket sells a large range of brands.
options.B: Workers already know how to sign up for overtime.
options.C: Saturday shifts are usually shorter than weekday shifts.
options.D: Most Saturday volunteers rely on their overtime payment for rent or travel and would have no practical way of exchanging the voucher for cash.
options.E: The supermarket sometimes gives shoppers money off seasonal goods.

questions.explanation: The workers most relevant to the prediction cannot use the substitute for the expenses they cover with cash. Equal face values therefore need not preserve the incentive.

questions.stem:
A music examination board found that applicants who submitted a video of their first attempt at a piece received lower marks than applicants who submitted a later attempt. It concludes that repeated attempts helped the second group improve their playing, rather than simply giving them another chance to record. The board is considering telling future applicants to rehearse with the camera running before making their final submission. Both groups played from the same list of pieces and were judged using the same published examination criteria.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: Applicants with more experience were much more likely to record several takes, and within each experience band the two groups' scores were similar.
options.B: The examination board permits applicants to practise without recording.
options.C: Some candidates needed help positioning a camera.
options.D: All the judges could identify the piece being played.
options.E: A later recording sometimes has better sound than an earlier one.

questions.explanation: Earlier experience could explain both why the applicants made repeated recordings and why they scored better. The within-band comparison directly challenges the causal claim.

questions.stem:
A coastal authority wants to prevent boats from damaging a shallow reef with their anchors. It proposes placing brightly coloured floating markers around the reef so that visiting skippers can see where anchoring is prohibited. The authority expects the markers to avert most damage, since owners rarely anchor deliberately in places they recognise as protected. Maps will continue to show the boundary, but the markers would be the first warning visible on the water. The patrol service would not be extended under this proposal.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: The new markers could be removed in winter.
options.B: Local boat owners sometimes report violations to the patrol service.
options.C: The reef is smaller than the authority originally estimated.
options.D: Most recorded damage occurred after dark, when the proposed markers would be invisible to skippers.
options.E: The authority's existing maps show the boundary accurately.

questions.explanation: The proposed mechanism is visual recognition. If the markers would not be seen at the time most damage occurs, they are unlikely to avert most damage.

questions.stem:
At a fish market, one seller has started placing a solid block of ice under each tray instead of spreading crushed ice around the fish. The seller reports that the blocks take longer to melt and on that basis claims they keep each fish cool for longer. The blocks and the crushed ice are made from the same water and start each morning at the same temperature. The market will recommend the new method to other sellers if it really improves the cooling of fish throughout the day.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: Blocks take less time to place in the trays.
options.B: Temperature probes showed that fish on blocks warmed sooner because most of their surfaces were not in contact with ice.
options.C: Ice makers can make blocks in several sizes.
options.D: Sellers normally clean their trays after the market closes.
options.E: The market sells a wider variety of fish in summer.

questions.explanation: The probes measure the claim that matters, the temperature of the fish. Slow melting is not enough if the ice is transferring less heat from the fish.

questions.stem:
A town held two local elections a year apart. In the second election it kept polling places open two hours later and recorded higher turnout. An officer argues that the additional hours were responsible and that the same change should be made permanent. She notes that the elections took place on the same day of the week and that residents voted at the same sites. The electoral register did grow slightly between the two elections, but the turnout figures were reported as proportions of registered voters rather than raw totals.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: Comparable nearby towns that did not extend their hours experienced turnout rises as large as this town's in the same elections.
options.B: Almost all polling places are accessible to wheelchair users.
options.C: Some staff volunteered to work during the extra hours.
options.D: A few voters registered shortly before the final deadline.
options.E: The ballot papers for both elections were printed locally.

questions.explanation: A comparable rise without extended hours points to an explanation shared by towns. The longer hours therefore cannot be inferred to be responsible from this comparison alone.

questions.stem:
A monument committee wants to replace several missing bronze fittings with new ones. A maker proposes using a cheaper alloy and argues that it will remain visually indistinguishable from the originals. In the workshop a freshly polished piece of the new alloy looks the same colour as a freshly polished sample from an original fitting. The proposed fittings would be installed on an exposed roof rather than kept in an indoor case. The committee intends to leave all the fittings untouched for many years once the repairs are finished.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: The new alloy is easier to cast into a complex shape.
options.B: Some of the old fittings still retain their original bolts.
options.C: In outdoor tests the new alloy darkened rapidly while the original alloy developed a much lighter coating.
options.D: Polishing a sample for display takes less than an hour.
options.E: Few visitors can see the underside of the roof.

questions.explanation: A match just after polishing does not imply a match after exposure. The tests directly contradict the proposed long-term match.

questions.stem:
A clinic has introduced a checklist to help a specialist decide which skin photographs require a closer examination in person. The specialist now recommends fewer examinations, and the manager says this shows that the checklist has cut unnecessary visits. The manager does not claim every photograph is clear, but notes that the cameras and referral requirements have stayed the same. The clinic has not yet compared what happened later to patients whose referrals were accepted with what happened to those who did not receive an in-person appointment.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: Staff find the new checklist quicker to complete than the former notes.
options.B: Many patients prefer an appointment to a telephone conversation.
options.C: The cameras have the same settings as last year.
options.D: A follow-up found that many referrals rejected under the checklist, but accepted under the old process, involved conditions that did need an in-person assessment.
options.E: Specialists sometimes consult a colleague before coming to a decision.

questions.explanation: The number of visits alone says nothing about whether those avoided were unnecessary. The follow-up establishes that important visits were among the ones lost.

questions.stem:
A publisher has tested a new typesetting program. During a two-week trial, designers completed straightforward pages faster than they did with their existing program. The publisher predicts that adopting the new software will reduce the time its teams spend preparing a typical full issue. The trial did not include pages that had to exchange files with outside illustrators, but the publisher notes that most pages do not require such exchanges. The price of the new software is no higher than the price of renewing the current licences.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: Outside illustrators generally submit invoice details separately from picture files.
options.B: Some designers would welcome a shorter training session.
options.C: Designers were told to record their working times in the trial.
options.D: The time lost on the few pages requiring outside files would exceed the time saved on all other pages in a typical issue.
options.E: The older program offers more page templates than designers regularly use.

questions.explanation: The conclusion concerns total preparation time, not the number of faster pages. A sufficiently costly exception reverses the overall saving.

questions.stem:
A town market association is considering requiring every stall to accept card payments. In a trial, three stalls began accepting cards and sold more goods than in the previous week. An adviser argues that the rule will raise the market's total takings, because some customers who have too little cash for a particular purchase can put it on their card instead. She expects these extra purchases to outweigh any fall in sales and assumes stallholders will not change their prices. The trial measured sales only at the three stalls, but the association wants to predict spending across the whole market rather than changes in which stalls customers favour.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.A: Customer diaries show that people buying more from the trial stalls cut their purchases at other market stalls by at least the same amount.
options.B: Stallholders who already accept cards usually wait a day for card receipts to reach their accounts.
options.C: Some trial customers with enough cash to make a purchase chose to use a card instead.
options.D: The association's figures do not include sales at permanent shops near the market.
options.E: Several stalls raised their takings during the trial by selling more expensive goods at unchanged prices.

questions.explanation: The trial could show a transfer of spending between stalls rather than additional spending across the market. The diaries directly support that explanation.

questions.stem:
Everyone who performs in the community orchestra is able to read music. How well they play is assessed, but the ability to read a score is also a condition of joining. On Thursday an organiser hears a new arrival at rehearsal read aloud the names of the notes on a page without making a mistake. There is no record of where this person has played before. The organiser concludes that the new arrival must already be a member of the orchestra, since only an orchestra member could meet its reading requirement.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It assumes that everyone in the orchestra plays the same instrument.
options.B: It confuses the order of the notes with their names.
options.C: It bases its conclusion on an overall average rather than an individual result.
options.D: It assumes that the orchestra has never added members.
options.E: It treats a condition for membership as sufficient evidence of membership.

questions.explanation: People outside the orchestra can read music too. The requirement establishes a one-way implication, which the organiser tries to reverse.

questions.stem:
An island newspaper profiles five sailors who won medals at a regatta. Every one of them says they made a point of checking the wind before launching, and each describes one occasion when doing so helped them. The newspaper did not speak to anyone who entered but failed to win a medal. The reporter concludes that a competitor who checks the wind is more likely to win than a competitor who does not, and advises newcomers to copy the medal winners' habit if they wish to improve their chances.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It assumes the competitors were all in separate races.
options.B: It gives no information about how often competitors who did not win also checked the wind.
options.C: It mistakes the winners' advice for a rule of the competition.
options.D: It assumes competitors who checked the wind cannot sail well without it.
options.E: It argues that because one sailor won, every sailor must have won.

questions.explanation: The winners alone provide no comparison group. Checking the wind could be just as common among competitors who never win.

questions.stem:
A town's tourism manager wants to know whether permanent street maps would help visitors find the station. In a trial, staff put up a map beside the main visitor gate and placed a volunteer next to it to explain the route. During the trial fewer people asked for directions in shops than in the previous week. The manager concludes that maps on their own will reduce the number of requests for directions. The permanent installations, however, would not be staffed, and the town has no plans to change shop opening hours.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It measures the number of people entering the gate rather than the questions asked in shops.
options.B: It assumes all shops are at the same distance from the station.
options.C: It uses evidence about shop staff to infer what shop customers prefer to buy.
options.D: It credits the map on the basis of a trial that also introduced someone to give directions.
options.E: It assumes people cannot find the station without assistance.

questions.explanation: The volunteer is a second intervention that might explain the fall. The trial does not isolate the effect of an unstaffed map.

questions.stem:
Some wax recordings from a historic speech collection are so faint that repeated playing would damage them before they could be transcribed. An archivist argues that none of the collection should be transcribed, because accurate transcripts of the faintest items could not be made safely. Several louder recordings in good condition are already playable on equipment in the archive. The proposed work would keep the original recordings whether or not transcripts were made, and it could proceed one recording at a time without affecting the condition of the others.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It extends a limitation of some recordings to the whole collection without justification.
options.B: It assumes that recordings can never be made from live speeches.
options.C: It treats an increase in available equipment as evidence of an increase in damage.
options.D: It appeals to the age of an archive to prove all the recordings are valuable.
options.E: It assumes transcripts must be made in the order in which the speeches were given.

questions.explanation: What is unsafe for the faintest items need not be unsafe for the playable ones. The argument overgeneralises from a subset.

questions.stem:
Households that installed heat pumps in a grant scheme had lower electricity bills on average last winter than households that kept electric heaters. A commentator concludes that every household in the grant scheme spent less on electricity than it would have spent with its old heater. The average was calculated from each household's complete bill, including electricity for cooking and lighting, and the scheme did not require households to send in bills from before installation. The commentator nevertheless says the averages establish that no participant could have lost money on electricity.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It assumes electricity was the only energy available in the district.
options.B: It compares total amounts when it should compare group averages.
options.C: It infers that grant participants are on average better cooks.
options.D: It infers an individual counterfactual saving for every household from a difference between group averages.
options.E: It takes a higher average bill to mean every device was used for longer.

questions.explanation: A lower average does not imply every participant had a lower bill. Nor do bills for other households show what any participant would have paid without changing heaters.

questions.stem:
A geologist tests a fragment brought to a lecture. Under ultraviolet light it gives off green light, a property that all known specimens of a particular rare mineral also display. Several common minerals can emit green light too, although geologists often distinguish these from the rare mineral by measuring hardness. The lecturer has not tested the fragment's hardness, but announces that it must be the rare mineral. She says that a reaction known to occur in every specimen is decisive evidence, even when it also occurs in other substances.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It uses hardness as a test after saying hardness is irrelevant.
options.B: It concludes that all light-emitting materials must be common.
options.C: It uses the audience's opinion as evidence of the fragment's composition.
options.D: It mistakes a property shared with the rare mineral for a property that identifies it uniquely.
options.E: It claims that because the mineral is rare no fragment could be an example of it.

questions.explanation: The emission is compatible with the rare mineral and with several alternatives. A necessary diagnostic property is not automatically a sufficient one.

questions.stem:
A tenants' panel offered residents two possible improvements to the entrances of a block: a ramp or better lighting. A petition for the ramp attracted more signatures than a separate petition for the lights. The panel concludes that more residents prefer the ramp to better lighting. The petitions were displayed at different times and residents were invited to sign either or both, but were not asked to rank the choices. They could also support one improvement without expressing any view about whether the other ought to take priority.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It assumes that the same resident could not sign both petitions.
options.B: It tries to infer which petition received more signatures from residents' preferences.
options.C: It assumes counts of endorsements establish residents' relative preferences between the options.
options.D: It objects to the ramp on the ground that lighting would be cheaper.
options.E: It treats the number of signatures as if it were the number of repairs completed.

questions.explanation: Signing one or both petitions states support, not a ranking, and the circumstances for signing differed. The totals therefore do not settle the relative preference.

questions.stem:
People who keep written records of how long they sleep report greater concern about their sleep than people who do not. A columnist infers that keeping a record makes people worried about sleeping, and suggests that anyone concerned should stop writing a sleep journal. The survey did not assign people either to keep a journal or to avoid doing so. It asked both groups the same questions and counted any regular written record, whether kept during a medical consultation or started privately, as a sleep journal.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It assumes the survey used different questions for the two groups.
options.B: It overlooks the possibility that concern about sleep prompts people to keep records rather than results from doing so.
options.C: It concludes that every reader will give up their journal.
options.D: It argues that a private journal must be more precise than a medical journal.
options.E: It objects to the survey because it did not count reports of concern.

questions.explanation: The correlation is consistent with people starting a journal because they are already worried. Without ruling that out, the columnist cannot infer the stated direction of cause.

questions.stem:
A town council is deciding whether to reproduce an old crest on a new civic building. A historian argues that a symbol should be used only if it can be understood by people who have no special knowledge of local history. An opponent says nobody in the town currently understands the old crest without guidance, so no symbol could meet the historian's test. Other designs have been suggested, including ones chosen for their plain imagery, but the opponent insists there is no need to discuss them before rejecting the test.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It assumes the new building will be used only by historians.
options.B: It wrongly infers that a symbol is old from the fact that it is hard to understand.
options.C: It takes the failure of one symbol to satisfy a test to show that no symbol could satisfy it.
options.D: It treats the historian's condition as a sufficient reason to choose a design.
options.E: It assumes that everyone who understands the existing crest approves of it.

questions.explanation: Even if the old crest fails the test, other designs might pass it. Evidence about one design cannot establish that the condition is impossible to meet.

questions.stem:
A sports league changed the points awarded for a win but left the rules of play unchanged. The season after the change, the total number of points awarded was greater. A commentator claims this proves teams played more aggressively, because aggressive play would lead to more wins and hence more points. The two seasons had the same number of matches, though the league does not report how many ended in a draw. The commentator says the total points are sufficient and does not seek any observations of how the teams actually played.

Which of the following best illustrates the flaw in the above argument?

options.A: It fails to distinguish between points awarded at home and points awarded away.
options.B: It treats a rise in an outcome affected by the scoring rule as evidence of a change in behaviour.
options.C: It reasons from evidence about the league as a whole to a claim about one named club.
options.D: It assumes the two seasons had different numbers of matches.
options.E: It ignores that a team which plays aggressively can sometimes lose as well as win.

questions.explanation: The scoring change can raise the points total even if match outcomes and behaviour stay the same. The observation therefore does not establish the proposed behavioural change.

questions.stem:
The panel that awards a research grant will review only proposals that include an estimate of running costs. The estimate lets the panel check that a project can continue after its equipment is bought. A chemist has submitted a proposal describing the equipment and the experiments, but it contains no estimate of running costs. The chemist's project might be promising and the panel might have enough money to fund it. Nonetheless, under the rule as it stands the proposal will not be reviewed.

Which of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.A: A race requires every entrant to wear a number. Lina is wearing a number, so she must be entered in the race.
options.B: A journal reads every submission with a summary. An article has a summary, so the journal will read it.
options.C: A gallery considers only submissions with a photograph. A sculptor submits no photograph, so the gallery will not consider the entry.
options.D: An office will print a form if it is signed. This form is not signed, so it cannot possibly print it.
options.E: The only person who can open the safe has a key. The safe is open, so that person must have used the key today.

questions.explanation: Review implies an estimate; without an estimate there is no review. The gallery option likewise uses the absence of a necessary condition.

questions.stem:
A hilltop beacon can be repaired only if its glass cover can be removed. The workshop manual says the cover can be removed only if the bolts holding it are released. The caretaker has now learnt that the bolts are fused solid and that nothing available on site can release them. The caretaker concludes that the beacon cannot be repaired on site this week. That conclusion does not depend on whether fixing the electrical fault inside the beacon would otherwise have been quick or whether a replacement bulb is already in stock.

Which of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.A: A loom can be started only if its guard closes, and the guard closes only if its latch moves freely. The latch is jammed, so the loom cannot be started.
options.B: A door opens whenever a latch is released. The latch has not been released, so the door is certainly shut.
options.C: A clock works if its battery is fitted, and the battery is fitted if there is a spare. There is a spare, so the clock works.
options.D: A gate has a guard only if it has a lock. The gate has a lock, so it has a guard.
options.E: A printer stops if its cover opens. The printer has stopped, so the cover must be open.

questions.explanation: The argument traces two requirements and rules out the final one. The loom example matches that chain from starting to closing to latch movement.

questions.stem:
A historian is trying to explain why the bells made in one town in the 1820s have similar decorative borders. A recently found notebook shows that a single mould maker supplied all the foundries responsible for those bells. If the foundries used the same mould maker, similar borders are what we would expect, because mould makers often reused their own designs. Independent copying of a fashionable pattern is still possible. The historian nevertheless thinks the shared supplier is a good explanation, without claiming that the pattern alone proves it.

Which of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.A: Several maps use the same colours, so they must have been drawn by the same person.
options.B: A coach planned sessions for two clubs, but the sessions differed; therefore the coach planned neither.
options.C: If a room leaks its wall will stain, but the wall is unstained, so the room does not leak.
options.D: A drawing was not attributed because its author is unknown, and no other drawing from the period should be attributed either.
options.E: Several old gardens have similar paths; all used the same designer, who often repeated a layout. The designer is a plausible explanation, although the owners might independently have copied a fashionable layout.

questions.explanation: Both infer a plausible common explanation supported by independent evidence while keeping another explanation open. They do not take the similarity as conclusive.

questions.stem:
To test frost damage, a grower divided a row of young plum trees into two groups. Both groups were watered and pruned in the same way, and they stood next to each other on equally exposed ground. One group alone was covered on the coldest nights. At harvest it had produced more undamaged fruit per tree than the uncovered group. The grower considers the protection the likeliest explanation for the difference, rather than attributing the result to the fact that the whole orchard was carefully looked after that year.

Which of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.A: Two groups of matching lamps run for the same hours. Only one group is fitted with heat shields and it has fewer failures, so the shields are the likeliest explanation.
options.B: Most swimmers who use different goggles are faster than last year, so the goggles must have helped.
options.C: Two teams practise together but win different numbers of matches, so practice does not affect results.
options.D: A classroom gains better lights and new blinds and pupils later report less glare, so the lights alone deserve the credit.
options.E: Recordings made on two different days differ in volume, so neither recording is reliable.

questions.explanation: In both cases two comparable groups differ in the proposed treatment, and the resulting difference provisionally supports that treatment's effect.

questions.stem:
A staff member claims a temperature alarm could not have sounded in a greenhouse last night because nobody at the estate office entered it in the alarm log. That in itself is not a good reason. There was no staff member at the office when the alarm is alleged to have sounded, and a person must hear the alarm there to enter it in the log. The lack of an entry is thus not useful evidence against the report. It does not follow that the report is true, either.

Which of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.A: A list omits some deliveries because staff disagreed about where to store them; therefore every delivery on it should be removed.
options.B: Nobody could have ordered a meal after the kitchen closed, because the only server had gone home.
options.C: A bird might have landed on an island despite being missing from a watcher's list, because nobody was on watch at the time. Its absence from the list does not settle the matter.
options.D: A camera recorded a fox in the garden, so it is wrong to say no fox visited.
options.E: A driver was not seen entering the bridge, so that driver must have taken another route.
